newsitem.title: CANADA: Royal Oak near resolving B.C. govt dispute.
newsitem.headline: Royal Oak near resolving B.C. govt dispute.

text.p: Royal Oak Mines Inc said on Monday it expects to resolve its dispute with the government of British Columbia this week over its Kemess copper-gold mine project.
But the Kirkland, Washington-based company is now in the midst of a second dispute, this time with the Northwest Territories Power Corp.

Gold production at Royal Oak's Giant gold mine in Yellowknife, Northwest Territories, was 17,000 ounces lower than expected in 1996, and costs were US$60 an ounce higher than expected, chairman Peggy Witte said in a conference call.
"This is a result of continued pressure put on us by the Northwest Territorial Power Corp with power rates. We're now paying the highest power rates anywhere in Canada," said Witte.
She said she had given the utility 20 days to lower its rates or the company would bring in its own generators to run the mine.
"We could be generating power there in the next two months," she said.
Costs would drop to about 7.5 Canadian cents per kilowatt hour from 11 cents on the generator system, she said.
Power accounted for about one third of the operating costs at the Giant mine, she added.
She said she expected to save C$1.5 million a year once it resolved the power dispute.
"It's a very serious issue for us," she said.
She also said police were investigating a motor breakdown at the Giant mine's mill that was responsible for shutting down the mill for three weeks in November.
"That motor failure is still under investigation because there appears to have been some sabotage that was involved with it," she said.
But Witte was optimistic that her company's dispute with the British Columbia government would be resolved this week.
Company officials had been negotiating with the government last week and today to resolve a dispute that Royal Oak had said threatened its Kemess project, she said.
The company's disagreement with the government centered on a 1995 agreement with the province compensating the company for the cancellation of the Windy Craggy copper project in British Columbia.
Royal Oak reported on Monday a loss of C$21.3 million or C$0.15 a share for the fourth quarter of 1996.
The results were a steep drop from a year earlier, when the company reported a net profit of C$3.7 million or C$0.03 a share.
Royal Oak blamed the drop on a fourth-quarter provision of C$37.6 million for the revaluation of its Hope Brook and Colomac mines and reclamation costs at Hope Brook.
Witte projected Royal Oak would produce 375,000 ounces of gold in 1997 at a cash cost of US$325 an ounce, versus 389,203 ounces in 1996 at a cash cost of US$343 an ounce.
Almost all 1997 production had been hedged at US$395 an ounce, Witte said.
She projected a 1997 gold price of about US$385 or US$390 an ounce.
"We certainly do see some strengthening in the gold market from where it is," she said.
But if the gold price dropped suddenly, the company would have to consider putting production at its Colomac mine on standby, she added.
((Heather Scoffield, Reuters Toronto Bureau 416 941-8104))
